explanationPatch.walkScript: Look at lines 4 to 6. Matthew barely notices that it is a girl. He slips past her without looking at her. Line 6 says that if he had looked, he would have seen how tense she was.

rebuilds.why: Hold (execution): the Nova Scotia distractor's execution carried boilerplate citing line 20 with a quotation cut off before the answer. Removed the boilerplate and pointed the execution at lines 20 and 21, where the stationmaster says what Mrs Spencer did. Nothing else changed.

options.value: She took the girl into her charge from him.

rebuilds.why: Hold (options): second defensible answer. Lines 14 to 18 tie the memory to the moment (a Gytrash came upon belated travellers, 'as this horse was now coming upon me'), so the travellers option was a reason the text gives. Repaired on the same stem, type and tier: the key now names the trigger the text gives (the horse coming upon her in the dusk, as in Bessie's tales), and the travellers option is replaced by an extreme-option distractor ('always ... every' tale true) that line 12 refutes ('rubbish'). Also named: the hint pointed at 'her age', which only the old key mentioned; replaced with a move. The walk now traces lines 11 to 18 to the new key.

stem.text: Read lines 11 to 18. Why does the Gytrash come into Jane's mind?

options.value: She had seen a Gytrash on this lane before.
options.execution: Lines 11 to 18 give her Bessie's tales, and no sighting of her own.

options.value: She had always believed every one of Bessie's tales was true.
options.execution: Stretches lines 11 to 13 into always and every. Line 12 counts the nursery stories among other rubbish, so the text is measured.

options.value: She was terrified of being alone in the lane.
options.execution: Line 11 gives fancies both bright and dark, which is not the same as terror.

options.value: A horse was coming upon her in the dusk, as in Bessie's tales.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Find where the tale comes back to her. Ask what is happening at that moment.
explanationPatch.walkScript: Lines 11 to 13 say that when she was young, her mind was full of fancies. At lines 14 and 15 a horse is coming through the dusk. Just then, line 15 says, she remembered Bessie's tales. Lines 16 and 17 say a Gytrash came upon travellers out late. Lines 17 and 18 say this horse was now coming upon her in the same way.

rebuilds.why: Hold (key): the key rested on reading 'however' (lines 22-23) as doubt, which the text never states, while line 25 says the rider 'broke the spell at once'; the walk invented a sentence and the hint pointed at the key. No small repair saves 'what FIRST makes her doubt', so the question is rewritten on the same passage, same questionType and tier: 'What tells Jane that this is no Gytrash after all?' The key is the rider (line 25: the man broke the spell; only a traveller). The old key (the dog passing quietly) is removed rather than kept as a distractor, since it is arguably a partial answer. Distractors: the colour (within the window, answers a different question), the fall on the ice (lines 28-29, after the spell is broken: chronology), and a tail-wag no line gives. New hint is a move; new walk cites lines 21 to 26.

stem.text: Read lines 21 to 26. What tells Jane that this is no Gytrash after all?

options.value: A man is riding the horse, and he is only a traveller.
Its black and white colour stood out against the trees.
options.execution: True at lines 20 and 21, but that is what made the dog easy to see. It does not tell her it is no Gytrash.

options.value: The horse and its rider slipped and fell on the ice.
options.execution: Man and horse fall at lines 28 and 29, after line 25 has already broken the spell. A later event is offered as the cause.

options.value: It wagged its tail at her as it went past.
options.execution: A friendly dog sounds ordinary, but no line in 21 to 26 has it wag its tail. Line 25 gives the rider as what broke the spell.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Find the line where the spell is broken. Read what comes just before it.
explanationPatch.walkScript: Lines 21 and 22 say the dog looked just like one form of the Gytrash. Lines 24 and 25 say the horse followed, with a rider on its back. Line 25 says the man broke the spell at once. Lines 25 and 26 say he was only a traveller on a short cut.

rebuilds.why: Hold (hintCore): 'He names two things. Keep both' matched only the key, the one option holding both (R572). Replaced with a move: read all of line 49 and check each option against every part of it. Nothing else changed.

He says that he shall do well enough.
options.execution: Reuses line 49, and that is what he claims, not what is the matter.

options.value: His shoulder was hurt when he came down.
options.execution: Line 49 names a sprain and line 50 has him try his foot; no shoulder appears.

explanationPatch.hintCore: Read all of what he says in line 49. Check each option against every part of it.

options.value: He is annoyed to find her out, and says so.

options.value: He questions her like a stranger, but knew of the governess.

options.value: She reports the light first, but describes little beyond what it shows.

options.execution: True at lines 30 and 31, and it is about her rather than about him.

rebuilds.why: Hold (key): a retrieval stem asked WHY he speaks low, but the passage gives no reason; line 37 is only the narrator's guess at the effect, so the key asserted an intent the text does not state, and one execution invented it too. options.value: Angrily, after losing his temper with her.

options.value: In a low voice that Miss Jenkyns probably could not hear.

rebuilds.why: Hold (options): 'It is only said that he was heard to say it' is the hearsay reason itself (line 50, 'It is said'), the same reason as the key in other words. stem.text: Look at lines 50 and 51. Why will the narrator not vouch for what she reports?

options.value: She thinks the Captain was right to say it.
options.execution: A plausible sympathy; lines 50 and 51 never give her a view on it at all.

options.value: She only has it at second hand from others.
She was staying in the house and did not dare.
options.execution: True at line 24, outside this window; that was about laughing, not about this. In the window, line 50 answers the stem: 'It is said—I won’t vouch for the fact—that Captain'.

options.value: The Captain was sorry afterwards and tried to make it up to her.
options.execution: Line 51 is inside the window and says that, if he did, he was penitent afterwards. That is what he did next, not why she will not vouch for the report.

stem.text: Look at lines 52 to 54. What does 'inexorable' on line 53 mean here?

options.value: Still in a fury with him about it.
options.execution: An adjacent state; line 53 gives an unmoving one rather than a hot one.

options.value: Not to be moved by anything he tried.
Trying to talk of some pleasanter thing.
options.execution: Lines 52 and 53 give that to the Captain, not to her.

rebuilds.why: Hold (hintCore): 'Two of these are things somebody said' was misleading, since the key paraphrases what Amy says at line 22, so a child could use the hint to rule the key out. stem.text: Look at lines 19 to 23. What does Amy think the burning has settled?

options.execution: Reuses line 22 and repeats her rather than saying what it settles.

options.value: That Jo meant to finish it before Father got home.
options.execution: True at lines 19 and 20, and it is Jo’s loss rather than Amy’s account.

options.value: That Jo has now paid for being cross to her.
That Jo will take her skating the next time.
options.execution: Amy wants skating later, at line 49, but lines 19 to 23 give no bargain. Line 22 is about paying Jo back.

rebuilds.why: Hold (key): the key ('easy enough to say at the table, and it is hard now') was unsupported: no line says the refusal was easy or that holding it is hard for Jo, lines 66 and 67 give her a bitter satisfaction, and there is no table (line 31 has a tea bell). Repaired on the same stem, type and tier: the key now says what the two moments do show, that she holds to her refusal even when it may put Amy in danger (line 70 the warning Amy misses; lines 72 and 73 the demon's words). The two distractors that said 'table' now say 'tea'; the 'forgotten' one is retagged en-contradicted-by-the-text (lines 66 and 67 say she cherished her anger), and the 'spoken then, warning later' one is retagged en-technique-structure-effect-blind (it reports content and order, not what the pairing shows). Walk rewritten to reach the key; it no longer claims Jo 'says nothing' at line 73. Gate-forced: the Laurie distractor's execution was under the precheck's 40-character minimum; it now adds that Laurie has already shouted the warning at line 70.

stem.text: Look at lines 33 to 35 and lines 68 to 73. What do the two moments show about Jo’s refusal?

options.execution: Lines 37 and 38 invite it; no line has her agree.

rebuilds.why: Hold (execution): the Laurie-testing execution said line 48 answers the stem and quoted line 48, which says nothing about the ice. Removed the boilerplate; it now cites lines 59 and 60 for Laurie sounding the ice and line 49 for what Amy says. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Look at lines 51 to 55. What does Meg tell Amy to wait for?

options.value: A quiet minute once Jo has cheered up.
That it is hard to forgive the loss of the book.
options.execution: Reuses lines 51 and 52 and gives Meg’s view rather than her instruction.

options.value: That she was very naughty.
options.execution: True at line 51, and it is Meg’s judgement rather than the advice.

options.value: Until Laurie has gone off home and left them alone.
options.execution: Lines 53 and 54 tell Amy to wait until Jo has got good-natured with Laurie, then take a quiet minute. The child supplies a different, likely condition, Laurie going home, which Meg never gives.

rebuilds.why: Hold (execution): the turned-her-back execution said line 64 answers the stem and quoted words about Amy. Removed the boilerplate; it now cites lines 58 and 59 for when Jo turned her back and line 65 for what Jo does while Amy puts her skates on. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Look at lines 64 to 66. What did Jo do while Amy put her skates on?

options.value: She stamped her feet and blew on her fingers.
options.execution: True at lines 64 and 65, and it is Amy rather than Jo.

options.value: She saw Amy coming and turned her back on her.
options.execution: True at lines 58 and 59, when Amy first reached the river. Line 65 gives what Jo does while Amy puts her skates on.

options.value: She went slowly down the river without turning.
She called out to Amy to hurry along after her.
options.execution: A sister waiting invites a shout; no line gives one.

rebuilds.why: Hold (execution): the 'under control from the table onwards' execution refuted it with lines 24 and 28, which come before tea (line 31). It now refutes it with lines 67 and 72, which come after. Nothing else changed.

stem.text: Think about the whole passage. How does the writer keep describing Jo’s anger?

options.value: Her hot temper mastered her, and she shook Amy.
options.execution: Reuses line 24 and quotes one moment instead of naming the pattern.

options.value: The writer tells us Jo is angry, but never shows the anger doing anything.
options.execution: Lines 24, 67 and 72 all have the anger doing something.

options.value: Jo has her anger under control from the table onwards, and keeps it there.
options.execution: Reverses who acts. After tea, line 67 has her anger take possession of her, and line 72 has a demon speak in her ear.

options.value: The anger is the one acting, but Jo is the one acted on.
